newsitem.title: VIETNAM: Hanoi seen keeping wary eye on China after Deng.
newsitem.headline: Hanoi seen keeping wary eye on China after Deng.

text.p: China's communist neighbour Vietnam remained silent in the early hours of Thursday morning following the death of paramount leader Deng Xiaoping, but analysts said Hanoi would be watching events in China closely.
Beijing's diplomatic compound was unlit overnight and police patrols said they had not been informed that Deng had died.
Flags throughout the city's main diplomatic quarter and area around the Ho Chi Minh mausoleum remained at full mast and state media carried no immediate mention of the news.
But diplomats and analysts said that while Deng Xiaoping's death was expected to have few immediate consequences for Hanoi, Vietnam would be scrutinising developments closely.
"They (the Vietnamese government) are well aware, through 4,000 years of history, of what a dynastic succession means," said a Western Vietnam watcher.

"At the moment it looks like Jiang Zemin is in charge, but the military may wish to show its strength at some point. Maybe it will be against Taiwan, maybe against the Spratlys. They (the Vietnamese) will know this."

The Spratlys are a potentially-oil rich series of reefs and islands in the South China Sea, whose sovereignty is claimed in whole or part by a number of regional countries including China and Vietnam.
Most observers said the full impact of Deng's death would depend on the fallout in China, and was therefore unlikely to be known for some time.

But they said a matter of immediate concern for Vietnam -- the recipient in recent years of a huge inflow of Chinese-related foreign investment pledges -- would be the impact on stock markets in Hong Kong, Taipei and Singapore.
Hanoi, however, was not expected to spend much time mourning Deng.

"There will be muted expressions of sorrow, but out of the sides of their faces," said a Western academic. "Everyone knows that he (Deng) was responsible for all the venom against Vietnam between 1978 and 1985."
The pragmatic reforms that Deng inspired in China swept south into Vietnam in the mid 1980s where they were officially adopted through a home grown version known as 'Doi Moi' or renovation.
At that time relations between Hanoi and Beijing were still soured from a bloody border war during the late 1970s and occasional frontier hostilities which were to continue for most of the 1980s.
More than a million people in Vietnam are ethnic Chinese.
Ties are seen as having improved in recent years with a growing number of top-level exchanges between the communist neighbours.
Deng became acquainted with the late president Ho Chi Minh during the 1920s, but the two men are said not to have got on, and he is not known to have visited Vietnam.
